Eusebius of Caesarea
yoo-SEE-bee-us
proper noun
Greek Eusebios, “pious” or “godly,” bishop of Caesarea in the early fourth century, called the father of church history.

See also: Eusebius of Caesarea

📖 Biblical Definition

Eusebius was bishop of Caesarea in Palestine in the early fourth century, and is justly called the father of church history. His Ecclesiastical History gathered the records of the church from the apostles to his own day, preserving for all later ages the testimony of the early writers, the succession of the churches, and above all the accounts of the martyrs who sealed their faith with blood. For this labour the dictionary owes him, as does every student of the early church, a great debt of gratitude. But Eusebius was no clear champion of the truth in the great controversy of his age. When Arius denied the full deity of the Son, Eusebius wavered, leaning to a subordinationism that fell short of the Scriptural confession that the Word was God, that He is before all things and by Him all things consist (Col 1:17), the brightness of the Father’s glory and the express image of His person (Heb 1:3). He subscribed the Nicene Creed only with reluctance, and ever after kept a courtier’s friendship with the powers of the world. The dictionary honours Eusebius as a historian without peer, while naming plainly the doctrinal weakness that kept him from standing with Athanasius for the eternal and equal Godhead of the Son, who said, Before Abraham was, I am (Joh 8:58).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The early fourth-century bishop of Caesarea, father of church history, but a waverer toward Arian subordinationism.

expand to see more

EUSEBIUS OF CAESAREA, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, the father of church history.

He flourished in the early fourth century under the emperor Constantine.

His Ecclesiastical History preserves the record of the early church and its martyrs.

He wavered in the Arian controversy toward a subordinationist view of the Son.

He subscribed the Nicene Creed only with reluctance.

📖 Key Scripture

Col 1:17 — "And he is before all things, and by him all things consist."

Heb 1:3 — "Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;"

Joh 8:58 — "Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am."

Joh 1:1 — "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

His history is of great price, but his subordinationism failed the deity of the Son that Nicaea confessed.

expand to see more

What is honourable in Eusebius is his history, which preserved for the church the testimony of its first three centuries and the precious record of the martyrs. The dictionary honours this labour and uses its fruit, as all later ages must.

The corruption to name is his doctrinal weakness. In the Arian controversy Eusebius leaned toward subordinationism, treating the Son as less than fully and eternally God, and he came to Nicaea’s confession of the Son as one substance with the Father only with a dragging reluctance. Scripture leaves no room for his hesitation: the Word was God, before all things, the brightness of the Father’s glory and the express image of His person, who said of Himself, Before Abraham was, I am. The dictionary honours Eusebius the historian while it refuses Eusebius the half-Arian, and marks how the courtier’s friendship with the throne too often dulls the edge of a man’s confession.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Greek for “godly,” Eusebius names the father of church history, a waverer in the Arian controversy.

expand to see more

Eusebius — Greek Eusebios, “pious” or “godly.”

He was bishop of Caesarea in Palestine in the early fourth century.

He is called the father of church history.

His Ecclesiastical History preserves the record of the early church.

He wavered toward Arian subordinationism in the great controversy.

Usage

"Like Eusebius, a man may serve the church greatly in one gift and fail it in another."

"The Son is before all things, and by Him all things consist; no subordinationism may stand."

"The courtier’s friendship with the throne too often dulls the edge of confession."
